notes.front: What is a sole proprietor?
notes.back: Someone who owns an unincorporated business by themselves.
notes.explanation: Publication 334 adds that an individual who is the only member of a domestic LLC is also a sole proprietor for income tax, unless the LLC elects corporate treatment.
notes.example: Like a freelance photographer who trades under their own name with no company formed: the business and the owner are one taxpayer.
notes.source: Publication 334 (2025), Tax Guide for Small Business, “Sole proprietor”, p. 3
notes.evidence: A sole proprietor is someone who owns an unincorporated business by themselves.

notes.front: What is a partnership for federal tax purposes?
notes.back: Generally, an unincorporated organisation with two or more members who carry on a trade, business, financial operation or venture and divide its profits.
notes.explanation: Publication 541 adds that a joint undertaking merely to share expenses is not a partnership.
notes.example: Like two friends who open a café together and split the profits, without forming a company.
notes.source: Publication 541 (Rev. December 2025), Partnerships, “Organizations Classified as Partnerships”, p. 2
notes.evidence: An unincorporated organization with two or more members is generally classified as a partnership for federal tax purposes if its members carry on a trade, business, financial operation, or venture and divide its profits.

notes.front: What is a qualified joint venture (QJV)?
notes.back: A business whose only members are spouses filing a joint return, which can elect not to be treated as a partnership.
notes.explanation: Both spouses must elect, and each then reports a share of the business as a sole proprietor.
notes.example: Like a married couple who run a bakery together in their own names, file jointly and choose not to file a partnership return.
notes.source: Publication 541 (Rev. December 2025), Partnerships, “Qualified joint venture”, p. 4
notes.evidence: A qualified joint venture, whose only members are spouses filing a joint return, can elect not to be treated as a partnership for federal tax purposes.

notes.front: Which business formed after 1996 is taxed as a corporation because of the law it was formed under?
notes.back: One formed under a federal or state law that refers to it as a corporation, body corporate or body politic.
notes.explanation: Publication 542 lists this first among the kinds of business formed after 1996 that are taxed as corporations.
notes.example: Like a company that files articles of incorporation with a state: the state law calls it a corporation, so the tax law does too.
notes.source: Publication 542 (Rev. January 2024), Corporations, “Businesses Taxed as Corporations”, p. 3
notes.evidence: A business formed under a federal or state law that refers to it as a corporation, body corporate, or body politic.

notes.front: What is an S corporation, and which form makes the election?
notes.back: A corporation (or entity eligible to be treated as one) that elects under section 1362(a); it elects on Form 2553.
notes.explanation: The same instructions set tests the entity must meet before it can make the election, covered on later cards.
notes.example: Like an ordinary corporation that has filed one extra election form to be taxed under a different set of rules.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 2553 (Rev. December 2020), “Purpose of Form”, p. 1
notes.evidence: A corporation or other entity eligible to elect to be treated as a corporation must use Form 2553 to make an election under section 1362(a) to be an S corporation.

notes.front: What is a limited liability company (LLC)?
notes.back: An entity formed under state law by filing articles of organisation as an LLC.
notes.explanation: Publication 541 contrasts it with a partnership: none of an LLC’s members are personally liable for its debts.
notes.example: Like a partnership in how it can be run, but the owners’ homes and savings are not on the line for the business’s debts.
notes.source: Publication 541 (Rev. December 2025), Partnerships, “Limited liability company (LLC)”, p. 3
notes.evidence: An LLC is an entity formed under state law by filing articles of organization as an LLC. Unlike a partnership, none of the members of an LLC are personally liable for its debts.

notes.front: What is a disregarded entity?
notes.back: An eligible entity with a single owner that is treated as not separate from its owner.
notes.explanation: Under the domestic default rule, a single-owner eligible entity is disregarded unless it elects otherwise on Form 8832.
notes.example: Like a one-owner LLC that exists under state law but whose income the tax law simply treats as the owner’s own.
notes.source: Form 8832 and Instructions, Entity Classification Election (Rev. December 2013), “Domestic default rule”, p. 5
notes.evidence: Unless an election is made on Form 8832, a domestic eligible entity is: 1. A partnership if it has two or more members. 2. Disregarded as an entity separate from its owner if it has a single owner.

notes.front: What is an eligible entity’s default classification?
notes.back: The federal tax classification it gets under the default rules when it files neither Form 8832 nor Form 2553.
notes.explanation: The Form 8832 instructions tell a new eligible entity that will use its default classification not to file Form 8832.
notes.example: Like the factory setting on a phone: it applies until you choose something else.
notes.source: Form 8832 and Instructions, Entity Classification Election (Rev. December 2013), “Purpose of Form”, p. 5
notes.evidence: A new eligible entity should not file Form 8832 if it will be using its default classification

notes.front: What is an exempt organization, as Publication 557 uses the term?
notes.back: An organisation recognised as exempt from federal income tax under section 501(a); these include those described in section 501(c).
notes.explanation: To qualify, the organisation must be organised for one or more of the purposes the Code specifically designates.
notes.example: Like a local food bank recognised as a charity: it exists for a purpose the Code names, so its income is not taxed.
notes.source: Publication 557 (Rev. January 2025), Tax-Exempt Status for Your Organization, “Introduction”, p. 3
notes.evidence: Organizations that are exempt under section 501(a) include those organizations described in section 501(c).

notes.front: What is an employer identification number (EIN)?
notes.back: A nine-digit number the Internal Revenue Service assigns (two digits, a hyphen, then seven) to identify the tax accounts of employers and certain others.
notes.explanation: Publication 1635 says it also identifies the tax accounts of certain others who have no employees.
notes.example: Like a social security number, but for a business’s tax accounts rather than a person.
notes.source: Publication 1635 (Rev. 2-2014), Understanding Your EIN, “What is an EIN?”, p. 4
notes.evidence: An Employer Identification Number (EIN) is a nine-digit number that IRS assigns in the following format: XX-XXXXXXX.

notes.front: What is a fiscal year?
notes.back: 12 consecutive months ending on the last day of any month except 31 December.
notes.explanation: A taxpayer allowed to adopt one must keep books and report income and expenses consistently on that period.
notes.example: Like a shop whose tax year runs from 1 July to 30 June, so the busy Christmas season falls mid-year.
notes.source: Publication 538 (Rev. January 2022), Accounting Periods and Methods, “Fiscal Year”, p. 3
notes.evidence: A fiscal year is 12 consecutive months ending on the last day of any month except December 31st.

notes.front: What is a 52-53-week tax year?
notes.back: An elected tax year that always ends on the same day of the week, so it runs 52 or 53 weeks.
notes.explanation: Publication 538 requires the year to end on the same weekday each time, tied to a chosen calendar month.
notes.example: Like a retailer whose year always ends on the last Saturday of January, so every year closes after a full week of trading.
notes.source: Publication 538 (Rev. January 2022), Accounting Periods and Methods, “52-53-Week Tax Year”, p. 3
notes.evidence: If you make this election, your 52-53-week tax year must always end on the same day of the week.

notes.front: What is a required tax year?
notes.back: A tax year required under the Internal Revenue Code and Treasury Regulations, which partnerships, S corporations and personal service corporations generally must use.
notes.explanation: The entity can avoid it with the Internal Revenue Service’s approval for another permitted year, or with a section 444 election.
notes.example: Like a school uniform: the rules pick it for you unless you get permission to wear something else.
notes.source: Publication 538 (Rev. January 2022), Accounting Periods and Methods, “Partnerships, S Corporations, and Personal Service Corporations (PSCs)”, p. 4
notes.evidence: A required tax year is a tax year that is required under the Internal Revenue Code and Treasury Regulations.

notes.front: What is Form W-2?
notes.back: The form an employer files to report employees’ wages, tips and other pay, and the income, social security and Medicare taxes withheld.
notes.explanation: Publication 334 lists it among the information returns a business with employees must file.
notes.example: Like an annual pay summary for each employee that also goes to the government.
notes.source: Publication 334 (2025), Tax Guide for Small Business, “Form W-2”, p. 12
notes.evidence: You must file Form W-2 to report payments to your employees, such as wages, tips, and other compensation, and withheld income, social security, and Medicare taxes.

notes.front: What is Form W-4?
notes.back: The employee’s withholding certificate: the signed form an employer uses to figure federal income tax withholding.
notes.explanation: Publication 15 tells employers to have a W-4 on file for each employee and to ask every new employee for a signed one.
notes.example: Like a set of instructions the employee hands payroll saying how much tax to take from each pay packet.
notes.source: Publication 15 (2025), (Circular E), Employer's Tax Guide, “Section 9, Income Tax Withholding”, p. 25
notes.evidence: Ask all new employees to give you a signed Form W-4 when they start work. Make the form effective with the first wage payment.

notes.front: What is Form 1099-NEC?
notes.back: Nonemployee Compensation: the information return a business files for people, not its employees, whom it paid for services.
notes.explanation: Publication 334 ties it to services by someone who is not your employee, among a few other payment types.
notes.example: Like a W-2 for a freelance web designer: it reports what the business paid them, but no wages.
notes.source: Publication 334 (2025), Tax Guide for Small Business, “Form 1099-NEC”, p. 12
notes.evidence: File Form 1099-NEC, Nonemployee Compensation, for each person in the course of your business to whom you have paid at least $600 during the year in: • Services performed by someone who is not your employee

notes.front: What is Form 1099-K?
notes.back: A form a business may receive showing the total dollar amount of its reportable payment card and third-party network transactions.
notes.explanation: It reports payment transactions, not the business’s income as such.
notes.example: Like a statement from a card processor or online payment app totalling what customers paid through it.
notes.source: Publication 334 (2025), Tax Guide for Small Business, “Payment card and third-party network transactions”, p. 21
notes.evidence: If you are in a business, you may receive a Form 1099-K representing the total dollar amount of total reportable payment transactions.

notes.front: For Part 2 sat between 1 July 2026 and 28 February 2027, which calendar year do questions relate to unless they say otherwise?
notes.back: 2025, with law as amended through 31 December 2025.
notes.explanation: The candidate bulletin also tells candidates to ignore legislation, court decisions and penalty amounts after 31 December 2025.
notes.source: IRS Special Enrollment Examination Candidate Information Bulletin (PSI, revised August 28, 2026), “Examination content”, p. 15
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In November 2026 a Part 2 question asks about a partnership’s filing duty for “the current tax year”. Which year’s rules apply?
notes.back: A: tax year 2025.
notes.choices:
A) Tax year 2025
B) Tax year 2026
C) Whichever year the partnership’s fiscal year ends in
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: the bulletin reads “current tax year” as calendar 2025 for this window. C is wrong: the phrase refers to the calendar year, not the entity’s own year.
notes.explanation: The bulletin defines “current tax year” as calendar 2025 for exams in this window.
notes.source: IRS Special Enrollment Examination Candidate Information Bulletin (PSI, revised August 28, 2026), “Examination content”, p. 15
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How many scored Part 2 questions cover Business Entities and Considerations?
notes.explanation: It is the second-largest of the three Part 2 domains.
notes.source: IRS Special Enrollment Examination Candidate Information Bulletin (PSI, revised August 28, 2026), “Examination Topics Overview”, p. 17
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How many scored Part 2 questions cover Business Tax Preparation?
notes.explanation: It is the largest of the three Part 2 domains.
notes.source: IRS Special Enrollment Examination Candidate Information Bulletin (PSI, revised August 28, 2026), “Examination Topics Overview”, p. 17
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How many scored Part 2 questions cover Specialized Returns and Taxpayers?
notes.explanation: It is the smallest of the three Part 2 domains; 30 + 37 + 18 makes the 85 scored questions.
notes.source: IRS Special Enrollment Examination Candidate Information Bulletin (PSI, revised August 28, 2026), “Examination Topics Overview”, p. 17
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does a sole proprietor report on Schedule C (Form 1040)?
notes.back: Income or loss from a business they operated or a profession they practised as a sole proprietor.
notes.explanation: Schedule C is part of the owner’s own Form 1040, not a separate business return.
notes.source: Instructions for Schedule C (Form 1040) (2025), “General Instructions”, p. 2
notes.evidence: Use Schedule C (Form 1040) to report income or (loss) from a business you operated or a profession you practiced as a sole proprietor.

notes.front: Dana is the only member of a domestic LLC that has never filed Form 8832. How is she treated for income tax?
notes.back: B: as a sole proprietor.
notes.choices:
A) As a partnership
B) As a sole proprietor
C) As a corporation
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: a partnership needs two or more members. C is wrong: corporate treatment needs an election, which Dana has not made.
notes.explanation: An individual who is the sole member of a domestic LLC is a sole proprietor unless the LLC elects corporate treatment.
notes.source: Publication 334 (2025), Tax Guide for Small Business, “Sole proprietor”, p. 3
notes.evidence: You are also a sole proprietor for income tax purposes if you are an individual and the sole member of a domestic LLC unless you elect to have the LLC treated as a corporation.

notes.front: Two neighbours co-own a flat that they rent out, providing no services to the tenant. Is the arrangement a partnership?
notes.back: B: no.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, because they share the rent
B) No, co-owned property that is merely rented out is not a partnership
C) Yes, once rent passes $10,000
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: sharing income from co-owned rented property is not enough without services to tenants. C is wrong: no rent threshold appears in the rule.
notes.explanation: Publication 541 says a joint undertaking merely to share expenses is not a partnership, giving co-owned rental property as the example.
notes.source: Publication 541 (Rev. December 2025), Partnerships, “Organizations Classified as Partnerships”, p. 2
notes.evidence: However, a joint undertaking merely to share expenses is not a partnership. For example, co-ownership of property maintained and rented or leased is not a partnership unless the co-owners provide services to the tenants.

notes.front: Spouses who file jointly own their landscaping business through a two-member LLC. Can it be a qualified joint venture?
notes.back: B: no.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, if both materially participate
B) No
C) Yes, if they file Form 8832
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: material participation is needed but not enough on its own. C is wrong: Form 8832 elects a classification; it does not create a qualified joint venture.
notes.explanation: A qualified joint venture must not be held in the name of a state law entity such as a partnership or an LLC.
notes.source: Publication 541 (Rev. December 2025), Partnerships, “Qualified joint venture”, p. 4
notes.evidence: the business is co-owned by both spouses and is not held in the name of a state law entity such as a partnership or an LLC.

notes.front: Besides filing jointly and co-owning the business, what must both spouses do for a qualified joint venture?
notes.back: Both elect not to be treated as a partnership, and both materially participate in the business.
notes.explanation: The requirements apply to each spouse, so one spouse’s participation does not satisfy the rule for both.
notes.source: Publication 541 (Rev. December 2025), Partnerships, “Qualified joint venture”, p. 4
notes.evidence: both spouses elect not to be treated as a partnership; both spouses materially participate in the trade or business

notes.front: A qualified joint venture earns $80,000 net; the spouses own it 60/40. How is the profit reported?
notes.back: A: $48,000 and $32,000 on separate Schedules C, with no Form 1065.
notes.choices:
A) $48,000 and $32,000 on separate Schedules C, with no Form 1065
B) $80,000 on one Form 1065
C) $40,000 each, whatever the ownership split
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: an electing qualified joint venture has no Form 1065 filing requirement. C is wrong: items are divided by the spouses’ respective interests, not equally.
notes.explanation: Items are split by each spouse’s interest ($80,000 × 60% = $48,000; $80,000 × 40% = $32,000), and each reports a share as a sole proprietor.
notes.source: Publication 541 (Rev. December 2025), Partnerships, “Qualified joint venture”, p. 4
notes.evidence: All items of income, gain, deduction, loss, and credit are divided between the spouses based on their respective interests in the venture. Each spouse takes into account their respective share of these items as a sole proprietor.

notes.front: A business incorporated in 2024 under a state law that calls it a “body corporate”. How is it taxed?
notes.back: C: as a corporation.
notes.choices:
A) As a partnership, if it has two owners
B) As a disregarded entity, if it has one owner
C) As a corporation
notes.choicesExplained: A and B are wrong: those default rules are for eligible entities; a business the state law calls a body corporate is taxed as a corporation.
notes.explanation: Publication 542 lists a business formed under a law that calls it a corporation, body corporate or body politic among those taxed as corporations.
notes.source: Publication 542 (Rev. January 2024), Corporations, “Businesses Taxed as Corporations”, p. 3
notes.evidence: A business formed under a federal or state law that refers to it as a corporation, body corporate, or body politic.

notes.front: A corporation has 99 unrelated individual shareholders plus a married couple who hold shares. Can it elect S status on the shareholder-count test?
notes.back: A: yes; the couple can count as one, giving 100.
notes.choices:
A) Yes; the couple can count as one, giving 100
B) No; it has 101 shareholders
C) No; married couples cannot hold S corporation stock
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: an individual and spouse can be treated as one shareholder. C is wrong: individuals are allowed shareholders, married or not.
notes.explanation: Counting the couple as one: 99 + 1 = 100, which is within the limit.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 2553 (Rev. December 2020), “Who May Elect”, p. 1
notes.evidence: You can treat an individual and his or her spouse (and their estates) as one shareholder for this test.

notes.front: A calendar-year corporation wants S status from 1 January 2025. What is the latest it can file Form 2553 during 2025 without needing late-election relief?
notes.back: A: 15 March 2025.
notes.choices:
A) 15 March 2025
B) 15 April 2025
C) 31 December 2025
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: that is 3 months and 15 days. C is wrong: a filing late in the year would take effect for the next year.
notes.explanation: The limit is 2 months and 15 days after the year begins: January and February, then 15 days of March. It could also have filed at any time during 2024.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 2553 (Rev. December 2020), “When To Make the Election”, p. 1
notes.evidence: No more than 2 months and 15 days after the beginning of the tax year the election is to take effect

notes.front: What are the three ways an LLC may be classified for federal income tax?
notes.back: A partnership, a corporation, or an entity disregarded as separate from its owner.
notes.explanation: The classification follows Treasury Regulations section 301.7701-3.
notes.source: Publication 542 (Rev. January 2024), Corporations, “Limited liability company (LLC)”, p. 3
notes.evidence: An LLC may be classified for federal income tax purposes as either a partnership, a corporation, or an entity disregarded as an entity separate from its owner

notes.front: A new domestic LLC with three members files no election. What is its default classification?
notes.back: A: a partnership.
notes.choices:
A) A partnership
B) A corporation
C) A disregarded entity
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: corporate treatment for an eligible entity needs an election. C is wrong: only a single-owner entity is disregarded by default.
notes.explanation: A domestic eligible entity with two or more members defaults to partnership status.
notes.source: Form 8832 and Instructions, Entity Classification Election (Rev. December 2013), “Domestic default rule”, p. 5
notes.evidence: Unless an election is made on Form 8832, a domestic eligible entity is: 1. A partnership if it has two or more members.

notes.front: A two-member LLC taxed as a partnership by default buys out one member, leaving one owner. What happens to its classification?
notes.back: It becomes a disregarded entity.
notes.explanation: The rule works both ways: a disregarded entity that gains a second member becomes a partnership.
notes.source: Form 8832 and Instructions, Entity Classification Election (Rev. December 2013), “Domestic default rule”, p. 5
notes.evidence: an eligible entity classified as a partnership will become a disregarded entity when the entity's membership is reduced to one member and a disregarded entity will be classified as a partnership when the entity has more than one member.

notes.front: Which new domestic LLC needs to file Form 8832?
notes.back: B: a single-member LLC that wants to be taxed as a corporation.
notes.choices:
A) A two-member LLC that wants partnership treatment
B) A single-member LLC that wants to be taxed as a corporation
C) A single-member LLC that wants to be disregarded
notes.choicesExplained: A and C are wrong: both want their default classification, and a new entity using its default should not file Form 8832.
notes.explanation: Form 8832 is filed by a domestic entity electing to be an association taxable as a corporation.
notes.source: Form 8832 and Instructions, Entity Classification Election (Rev. December 2013), “Who Must File”, p. 6
notes.evidence: A domestic entity electing to be classified as an association taxable as a corporation.

notes.front: How far before and after the filing date can a Form 8832 election take effect?
notes.back: No more than 75 days before the filing date, and no later than 12 months after it.
notes.explanation: The effective date is the date on line 8, or the filing date if none is entered.
notes.source: Form 8832 and Instructions, Entity Classification Election (Rev. December 2013), “Line 8”, p. 7
notes.evidence: An election specifying an entity's classification for federal tax purposes can take effect no more than 75 days prior to the date the election is filed, nor can it take effect later than 12 months after the date on which the election is filed.

notes.front: An LLC files Form 8832 on 1 June 2025, entering 1 January 2025 on line 8. When does the election take effect?
notes.back: B: 18 March 2025.
notes.choices:
A) 1 January 2025
B) 18 March 2025
C) 1 June 2025
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: that is more than 75 days before filing. C is wrong: the election does not fall back to the filing date.
notes.explanation: A date more than 75 days early defaults to 75 days before filing: back 31 days to 1 May, 30 to 1 April, 14 more to 18 March.
notes.source: Form 8832 and Instructions, Entity Classification Election (Rev. December 2013), “Line 8”, p. 7
notes.evidence: If line 8 shows a date more than 75 days prior to the date on which the election is filed, the election will default to 75 days before the date it is filed.

notes.front: After an entity elects to change its classification, how long must it generally wait before changing again by election?
notes.back: 60 months after the effective date of the election.
notes.explanation: An earlier change may be allowed by private letter ruling if more than 50% of the ownership is new.
notes.source: Form 8832 and Instructions, Entity Classification Election (Rev. December 2013), “Lines 2a and 2b. 60-month limitation rule”, p. 7
notes.evidence: Once an eligible entity makes an election to change its classification, the entity generally cannot change its classification by election again during the 60 months after the effective date of the election.

notes.front: Churches, hospitals, museums, schools and scientific research organisations are charities described in which section?
notes.back: Section 501(c)(3).
notes.explanation: Publication 557 lists them together with other charities under that section.
notes.source: Publication 557 (Rev. January 2025), Tax-Exempt Status for Your Organization, “Tax-exempt entities”, p. 60
notes.evidence: Churches, hospitals, museums, schools, scientific research organizations, and other charities described in section 501(c)(3)

notes.front: Which two kinds of taxpayer, besides employers, use EINs? Name two.
notes.back: Any two, among others: for example, sole proprietors and trusts.
notes.explanation: Publication 1635 also lists sole proprietors, corporations, partnerships, non-profit associations, estates, government agencies and certain individuals.
notes.source: Publication 1635 (Rev. 2-2014), Understanding Your EIN, “What is an EIN?”, p. 4
notes.evidence: EINs are used by employers, sole proprietors, corporations, partnerships, non-profit associations, trusts, estates of decedents, government agencies, certain individuals, and other business entities.

notes.front: Can a sole proprietor use their EIN in place of their social security number?
notes.back: No. An EIN is for business activities only.
notes.explanation: Publication 1635 says the EIN is for use in connection with business activities.
notes.source: Publication 1635 (Rev. 2-2014), Understanding Your EIN, “What is an EIN?”, p. 4
notes.evidence: An EIN is for use in connection with your business activities only. Do not use your EIN in place of your social security number (SSN).

notes.front: A sole proprietor with an EIN incorporates the business. Does the corporation need a new EIN?
notes.back: Yes. Incorporating is one of the events that needs a new EIN.
notes.explanation: The same list includes a sole proprietor taking in partners and operating as a partnership.
notes.source: Publication 1635 (Rev. 2-2014), Understanding Your EIN, “Sole Proprietors”, p. 5
notes.evidence: You will need a new EIN if any of the following are true: • You file bankruptcy under Chapter 7 (liquidation) or Chapter 11 (reorganization) of the Bankruptcy Code • You incorporate •

notes.front: A sole proprietor takes in two partners and carries on as a partnership. New EIN?
notes.back: Yes. The business now needs a new EIN.
notes.explanation: Publication 1635 lists it, with incorporating, among the events that need a new EIN for a sole proprietor.
notes.source: Publication 1635 (Rev. 2-2014), Understanding Your EIN, “Sole Proprietors”, p. 5
notes.evidence: You are a sole proprietor and take in partners and operate as a partnership

notes.front: A sole proprietor renames the business and opens a second shop. New EIN?
notes.back: No. A name change or an added location does not need a new EIN.
notes.explanation: Publication 1635 lists both among the changes that do not need a new EIN.
notes.source: Publication 1635 (Rev. 2-2014), Understanding Your EIN, “Sole Proprietors”, p. 5
notes.evidence: You do not need a new EIN if any of the following are true: • You change the name of your business • You change your location or add locations

notes.front: When does an applicant get an EIN applied for online?
notes.back: Immediately, once the online application is completed.
notes.explanation: Publication 1635 calls the online application the preferred method.
notes.source: Publication 1635 (Rev. 2-2014), Understanding Your EIN, “Apply Online”, p. 16
notes.evidence: Once you've completed the application, you will receive your EIN immediately.

notes.front: What is a calendar tax year?
notes.back: 12 consecutive months beginning on 1 January and ending on 31 December.
notes.explanation: A taxpayer who adopts it keeps books and reports income and expenses for that same period.
notes.source: Publication 538 (Rev. January 2022), Accounting Periods and Methods, “Calendar Year”, p. 2
notes.evidence: A calendar year is 12 consecutive months beginning on January 1st and ending on December 31st.

notes.front: Can an individual sole proprietor use a tax year ending 30 September?
notes.back: Yes, but only if they keep their books and records on the basis of that fiscal year.
notes.explanation: Individuals generally must adopt the calendar year.
notes.source: Publication 538 (Rev. January 2022), Accounting Periods and Methods, “Individuals”, p. 4
notes.evidence: Generally, individuals must adopt the calendar year as their tax year. An individual can adopt a fiscal year if the individual maintains his or her books and records on the basis of the adopted fiscal year.

notes.front: Which of these tax years is a fiscal year?
notes.back: B: 1 May 2025 to 30 April 2026.
notes.choices:
A) 1 January to 31 December 2025
B) 1 May 2025 to 30 April 2026
C) 15 March 2025 to 14 March 2026
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: a year ending 31 December is a calendar year. C is wrong: a fiscal year ends on the last day of a month.
notes.explanation: A fiscal year must end on the last day of a month other than December.
notes.source: Publication 538 (Rev. January 2022), Accounting Periods and Methods, “Fiscal Year”, p. 3
notes.evidence: A fiscal year is 12 consecutive months ending on the last day of any month except December 31st.

notes.front: Partners holding 60% of a partnership’s profits and capital all use a 30 June year end. What tax year must the partnership use?
notes.back: A: the year ending 30 June.
notes.choices:
A) The year ending 30 June
B) The calendar year
C) Any year it chooses
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: the calendar year is not automatic for a partnership. C is wrong: a partnership must use its required tax year unless an exception applies.
notes.explanation: Partners with the same year who own more than 50% of profits and capital set the required year.
notes.source: Publication 538 (Rev. January 2022), Accounting Periods and Methods, “Partnership”, p. 5
notes.evidence: If one or more partners having the same tax year own a majority interest (more than 50%) in partnership profits and capital, the partnership must use the tax year of those partners.

notes.front: If no majority-interest tax year exists, whose tax year must a partnership use next?
notes.back: The tax year of all its principal partners: those with 5% or more of profits or capital.
notes.explanation: This is the second step in the order of tests for a partnership’s required year.
notes.source: Publication 538 (Rev. January 2022), Accounting Periods and Methods, “Partnership”, p. 5
notes.evidence: If there is no majority interest tax year, the partnership must use the tax year of all its principal partners. A principal partner is one who has a 5% or more interest in the profits or capital of the partnership.

notes.front: Which tax year is not on the list of permitted years for an S corporation?
notes.back: C: a year ending 30 April chosen with no election and no business purpose.
notes.choices:
A) The calendar year
B) A year elected under section 444
C) A year ending 30 April chosen with no election and no business purpose
notes.choicesExplained: A and B are wrong: both are permitted tax years, as is a year with an established business purpose.
notes.explanation: All S corporations must use a permitted tax year, which Publication 538 lists as the calendar year, a section 444 year, a related 52-53-week year, or a business-purpose year.
notes.source: Publication 538 (Rev. January 2022), Accounting Periods and Methods, “S Corporation”, p. 5
notes.evidence: All S corporations, regardless of when they became an S corporation, must use a permitted tax year.

notes.front: What tax year must a personal service corporation generally use?
notes.back: The calendar year, unless an exception applies, such as a section 444 election.
notes.explanation: It is one of the entities, with partnerships and S corporations, that generally must use a required tax year.
notes.source: Publication 538 (Rev. January 2022), Accounting Periods and Methods, “Personal Service Corporation (PSC)”, p. 6
notes.evidence: A PSC must use a calendar tax year unless any of the following apply. • The corporation makes an election under section 444

notes.front: Which form makes a section 444 election to use a tax year other than the required tax year?
notes.back: Form 8716.
notes.explanation: It is filed with the service centre where the entity will file its return, and a copy goes with the first return for the year.
notes.source: Publication 538 (Rev. January 2022), Accounting Periods and Methods, “Section 444 Election”, p. 6
notes.evidence: Make a section 444 election by filing Form 8716 with the Internal Revenue Service Center where the entity will file its tax return.

notes.front: Which form generally requests approval from the Internal Revenue Service to change a tax year?
notes.back: Form 1128.
notes.explanation: The Form 1128 instructions list exceptions, and automatic approval requests need no user fee.
notes.source: Publication 538 (Rev. January 2022), Accounting Periods and Methods, “Change in Tax Year”, p. 4
notes.evidence: Generally, you must file Form 1128 to request IRS approval to change your tax year.

notes.front: By what date must an employer give employees their Form W-2, and file W-2 and W-3 with the Social Security Administration?
notes.back: 31 January for both, moved to the next business day when it falls on a weekend or holiday.
notes.explanation: Table 1-2 gives 31 January for both, with a footnote moving weekend dates on. For 2025 forms, 31 January 2026 is a Saturday, so both are due Monday 2 February 2026.
notes.source: Publication 334 (2025), Tax Guide for Small Business, “Table 1-2. Which Forms Must I File?”, p. 11
notes.evidence: W-2 (to employee) January 31.3 W-2 and W-3 (to the SSA) January 31

notes.front: A café paid three employees during 2025. By when must it hand each their 2025 Form W-2?
notes.back: A: 2 February 2026.
notes.choices:
A) 2 February 2026
B) 15 April 2026
C) 31 March 2026
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: 15 April is an individual return date, not a W-2 date. C is wrong: 31 March 2026 is the e-file date for most Forms 1099, not Forms W-2.
notes.explanation: The usual date is 31 January, but 31 January 2026 is a Saturday. A due date on a weekend moves to the next business day: Monday 2 February 2026.
notes.source: Publication 334 (2025), Tax Guide for Small Business, “Table 1-2. Which Forms Must I File?”, p. 11
notes.evidence: If a due date falls on a Saturday, Sunday, or legal holiday, file by the next day that is not a Saturday, Sunday, or legal holiday.

notes.front: A new employee starts in 2025 but never hands in a Form W-4. How does the employer withhold?
notes.back: As if the employee checked single or married filing separately and made no other entries.
notes.explanation: Publication 15 sets this default for new employees without a completed 2025 Form W-4, including rehired ones.
notes.source: Publication 15 (2025), (Circular E), Employer's Tax Guide, “Section 9, Income Tax Withholding”, p. 25
notes.evidence: treat the new employee as if they had checked the box for Single or Married filing separately in Step 1(c) and made no entries in Step 2, Step 3, or Step 4 of the 2025 Form W-4.

notes.front: For 2025, a business must file Form 1099-NEC for a person it paid at least how much for services by a non-employee?
notes.back: $600 during the year.
notes.explanation: Tax year 2025 is what the exam tests; Publication 334 (2025) gives this threshold.
notes.source: Publication 334 (2025), Tax Guide for Small Business, “Form 1099-NEC”, p. 12
notes.evidence: File Form 1099-NEC, Nonemployee Compensation, for each person in the course of your business to whom you have paid at least $600 during the year

notes.front: In 2025 a sole proprietor paid a freelance designer $450 and a bookkeeper (not an employee) $700. No tax was withheld. Which need a Form 1099-NEC?
notes.back: B: only the bookkeeper.
notes.choices:
A) Both
B) Only the bookkeeper
C) Neither
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: $450 is under the $600 threshold. C is wrong: $700 is at least $600.
notes.explanation: Compare each payee to $600: $450 < $600, so no form; $700 ≥ $600, so a form is needed.
notes.source: Publication 334 (2025), Tax Guide for Small Business, “Form 1099-NEC”, p. 12
notes.evidence: File Form 1099-NEC, Nonemployee Compensation, for each person in the course of your business to whom you have paid at least $600 during the year

notes.front: By what date must 2025 Forms 1099-NEC be filed?
notes.back: 2 February 2026.
notes.explanation: The general instructions for 2025 information returns give this date with a caution symbol.
notes.source: General Instructions for Certain Information Returns (2025), “Due dates”, p. 8
notes.evidence: File Form 1099-NEC by February 2, 2026.

notes.front: A client asks whether 2025 Forms 1099-NEC can be e-filed with other Forms 1099 by 31 March 2026. What do you tell them?
notes.back: C: No; Form 1099-NEC is due 2 February 2026.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, all Forms 1099 are due 31 March if e-filed
B) Yes, if the payees agree
C) No; Form 1099-NEC is due 2 February 2026
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: 31 March 2026 is the e-file date for most Forms 1099, but not the 1099-NEC. B is wrong: payees cannot change a filing due date.
notes.explanation: The 2025 general instructions set 2 February 2026 for Form 1099-NEC, separately from the 31 March date for most Forms 1099.
notes.source: General Instructions for Certain Information Returns (2025), “Due dates”, p. 8
notes.evidence: E-file Forms 1097, most Forms 1098, and most Forms 1099, 3921, 3922, or W-2G by March 31, 2026.

notes.front: A shop’s Form 1099-K shows $52,000, which includes $2,000 of sales tax collected. Should it simply report $52,000 as gross receipts?
notes.back: No. The 1099-K total may include items that are not receipts, such as sales tax, and may miss some receipts.
notes.explanation: Publication 334 warns that the 1099-K amount may not be the amount to report as income.
notes.source: Publication 334 (2025), Tax Guide for Small Business, “Payment card and third-party network transactions”, p. 21
notes.evidence: This may not be the amount you should report as income, as it may not include all the receipts and it may include items that are not included in your receipts (such as sales tax).

notes.front: According to the Schedule C instructions, when does an activity qualify as a business?
notes.back: When your primary purpose is income or profit and you are involved with continuity and regularity.
notes.explanation: A sporadic activity, a not-for-profit activity or a hobby does not qualify.
notes.source: Instructions for Schedule C (Form 1040) (2025), “General Instructions”, p. 2
notes.evidence: An activity qualifies as a business if your primary purpose for engaging in the activity is for income or profit and you are involved in the activity with continuity and regularity.

notes.front: Which factors are considered in deciding whether a farming activity is carried on for profit? Name two.
notes.back: Any two, among others: for example, running it in a businesslike manner and depending on its income for a livelihood.
notes.explanation: Publication 225 lists nine factors, including the time and effort spent and changes of method to improve profitability.
notes.source: Publication 225 (2025), Farmer's Tax Guide, “Not-for-Profit Farming”, p. 29
notes.evidence: You operate your farm in a businesslike manner; • The time and effort you spend on farming indicate you intend to make it profitable; • You depend on income from farming for your livelihood;

notes.front: When is an activity presumed to be carried on for profit?
notes.back: If it produced a profit in at least 3 of the last 5 tax years, including the current year.
notes.explanation: For horse breeding, training, showing or racing the test is 2 of the last 7 years.
notes.source: Publication 225 (2025), Farmer's Tax Guide, “Presumption of profit”, p. 29
notes.evidence: Your farming or other activity is presumed carried on for profit if it produced a profit in at least 3 of the last 5 tax years, including the current year.

notes.front: A pottery activity had profits in 2021 and 2023, and losses in 2022, 2024 and 2025. Is it presumed to be for profit in 2025?
notes.back: B: no; only 2 of the last 5 years show a profit.
notes.choices:
A) Yes; it has made a profit before
B) No; only 2 of the last 5 years show a profit
C) Yes; 2 of 7 years is enough
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: the test counts profit years in the last five, not any profit. C is wrong: the 2-of-7 test is only for horse activities.
notes.explanation: Counting 2021–2025: two profit years, fewer than the three required.
notes.source: Publication 225 (2025), Farmer's Tax Guide, “Presumption of profit”, p. 29
notes.evidence: Your farming or other activity is presumed carried on for profit if it produced a profit in at least 3 of the last 5 tax years, including the current year.

notes.front: Can a loss from an activity not carried on for profit generally offset other income?
notes.back: No.
notes.explanation: Hobbies and activities mainly for sport or recreation come under this limit.
notes.source: Publication 334 (2025), Tax Guide for Small Business, “Activities Not Engaged in for Profit”, p. 43
notes.evidence: You generally can't use a loss from the activity to offset other income. Activities you do as a hobby, or mainly for sport or recreation, come under this limit.

notes.front: Lee breeds show rabbits as a hobby: $3,000 of sales and $5,000 of costs in 2025. What does Lee report?
notes.back: C: $3,000 of income on Schedule 1, line 8j, with no deduction for the $5,000.
notes.choices:
A) A $2,000 loss on Schedule C
B) Nothing, since costs exceed sales
C) $3,000 of income on Schedule 1, line 8j, with no deduction for the $5,000
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: a hobby is not a business, so it does not go on Schedule C, and its loss cannot offset other income. B is wrong: hobby income is still reported.
notes.explanation: Income from a not-for-profit activity goes on Schedule 1, line 8j, and its expenses can no longer be deducted, even by itemisers.
notes.source: Publication 225 (2025), Farmer's Tax Guide, “Not-for-Profit Farming”, p. 28
notes.evidence: you report the income from the activity on Schedule 1 (Form 1040), line 8j. You can no longer deduct expenses of carrying on the activity, even if you itemize your deductions on Schedule A (Form 1040).

notes.front: A sole proprietor runs the business through a single-member LLC and has no employment or excise tax returns to file. Does the LLC need its own EIN?
notes.back: No. It needs a separate EIN only if it must file employment or excise tax returns.
notes.explanation: Publication 1635 contrasts this with events like incorporating, which do need a new EIN.
notes.source: Publication 1635 (Rev. 2-2014), Understanding Your EIN, “Sole Proprietors”, p. 5
notes.evidence: who conducts business as a limited liability company (LLC), you do not need a separate EIN for the LLC, unless you are required to file employment or excise tax returns.
